Consistency tests in depth

Source: vignettes/consistency-tests-in-depth.Rmd
consistency-tests-in-depth.Rmd

Introduction

This vignette describes scrutiny’s infrastructure for implementing new consistency tests.

A consistency test is implemented at several levels, most of them created from the previous one by a function factory. Since the factories work the same way for every test, all test functions share one interface: anyone who knows the grim_*() functions can use the grimmer_*() functions as well.

These are the levels, with GRIM as the example. If you implement a valid consistency test at least at the first level, I’ll be happy to accept a pull request to scrutiny.

  1. A non-exported function that tests a single case, such as grim_scalar().

  2. A vectorized version of it, such as grim().

  3. A mapper that applies the single-case function to each row of a data frame, such as grim_map().

  4. An audit() method that summarizes the output of number 3, and an explain_map() method that explains it.

  5. A function that plots the output of number 3, such as grim_plot_grid().

  6. A sequence mapper that tests slightly varied input values, such as grim_map_seq().

  7. A total-n mapper for studies with two groups that only report the total sample size, such as grim_map_total_n().

The examples use a mock test called SCHLIM, which has no meaning in itself. A real implementation will usually be more complex than the snippets below.

Please follow the tidyverse style guide and the conventions below. To write a new package, see R Packages (Wickham and Bryan 2023).

1. Single-case

This function contains the test itself. It is not exported, but every other level builds on it.

It takes one value for each statistic that is tested for consistency with the others. It returns TRUE if they are consistent, FALSE if they aren’t, and NA if the case can’t be decided, as with a missing value. In scrutiny’s own tests, a missing value only makes the result NA if some value in its place would make the case consistent and another would not; see Missing values in vignette("technical-notes").

schlim_scalar <- function(y, n) {
  (y / 3) > n
}

schlim_scalar(y = 30, n = 4)
#> [1] TRUE
schlim_scalar(y = 2, n = 7)
#> [1] FALSE

If the test reconstructs rounded numbers, give the function a rounding argument with the default "up_or_down", and pass it on to roundwork::reround() or roundwork::unround(); see vignette("rounding-in-depth", package = "roundwork"). To compare the range of a rounded value with whole numbers, as GRIM does, use roundwork::bound_numerators() or roundwork::sum_range(), which keep the comparison exact; see Exact arithmetic in vignette("technical-notes"). Take the number of decimal places as an argument without a default, like digits_x in grim(), rather than counting them: a numeric value has lost any trailing zeros.

decimal_places() counts the digits after the decimal point or another separator. It takes numbers and strings, and it is vectorized:

decimal_places("2.80")
#> [1] 2

decimal_places(c(55.1, 6.493, 8))
#> [1] 1 3 0

Numeric values drop trailing zeros, whereas strings preserve them. This is why the consistency tests take the number of decimal places as an argument rather than counting it:

decimal_places(7.200)
#> [1] 1

decimal_places("7.200")
#> [1] 3

Name the function after the test in lowercase, followed by _scalar. If R’s own vectorization already makes it work on vectors in every argument, leave out _scalar, export it, and skip section 2.

Exported scrutiny functions often call internal helpers, most of which are documented in utils.R. To reuse one, copy its source code, which scrutiny:::helper_name (without parentheses) prints. Don’t call it with ::: in your code: internals can change or vanish without notice. See this blogpost by Thomas Lin Pedersen.

2. Vectorized

The simplest way to vectorize the single-case function is Vectorize(). The result is named after the test:

schlim <- Vectorize(schlim_scalar)

schlim(y = 10:15, n = 4)
#> [1] FALSE FALSE FALSE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE

Vectorize() loops over every argument. This is wrong for two kinds of arguments: those that only the mapper should set, such as show_rec in grim_scalar(), which makes the function return a list; and those that describe the test as a whole, such as rounding. This is why grim(), grimmer(), and debit() have handwritten signatures instead. If your single-case function has such arguments, do the same: loop over the reported values only, and pass the other arguments on as they are. Suppose schlim_scalar() took a rounding argument:

schlim <- function(y, n, rounding = "up_or_down") {
  purrr::map2_lgl(y, n, schlim_scalar, rounding = rounding)
}

purrr::map2_lgl() recycles only values of length 1, so y and n must otherwise have the same length. Use purrr::pmap_lgl() for three or more reported values.

The rest of the vignette builds on the mapper, not on the vectorized function.

3. Basic mapper

Creating basic mappers with function_map()

A mapper applies the test to every row of a data frame, as grim_map() does. Every function in the rest of the vignette builds on it. It accepts any data frame and returns a tibble.

Create mappers with function_map():

schlim_map <- function_map(
  .fn = schlim_scalar,
  .reported = c("y", "n"),
  .name_test = "SCHLIM"
)

# Example data:
df1 <- tibble::tibble(y = 16:25, n = 3:12)

schlim_map(df1)
#> # A tibble: 10 × 3
#>        y     n consistency
#>    <int> <int> <lgl>      
#>  1    16     3 TRUE       
#>  2    17     4 TRUE       
#>  3    18     5 TRUE       
#>  4    19     6 TRUE       
#>  5    20     7 FALSE      
#>  6    21     8 FALSE      
#>  7    22     9 FALSE      
#>  8    23    10 FALSE      
#>  9    24    11 FALSE      
#> 10    25    12 FALSE

These arguments are required:

  • .fn is the single-case function from section 1.

  • .reported names the arguments of .fn that take the reported statistics. These become the key columns. function_map() does not assume any particular number of them: GRIM has two, GRIMMER and DEBIT have three.

  • .name_test is the name of the test, used in messages and in the class of the output.

Every other argument of .fn becomes an argument of the mapper, with the same default. Optional arguments of function_map() control how some of them are treated:

Argument Purpose Example in scrutiny
.args_by_row Arguments that take one value per row, returned as columns digits_x
.cols_helper Arguments that may also be columns of data, returned after the key columns if given items_averaged
.args_fixed Values always passed to .fn; the mapper has no argument for them list(show_reason = TRUE) in grimmer_map()
.args_disabled Arguments of .fn that the mapper should not have
.col_names Names of the columns that a list returned by .fn unpacks into; the first is the key result show_rec = TRUE columns
.cols_derived Vectorized functions that compute further columns from the same columns list(exp_incon = grim_exp_incon)
.name_class Extra classes for the output
.name_key_result Name of the result column, "consistency" by default

grim_map() itself is made this way:

grim_map <- function_map(
  .fn = grim_scalar,
  .reported = c("x", "n"),
  .name_test = "GRIM",
  .args_by_row = "digits_x",
  .cols_helper = c("items_averaged", "data_type"),
  .col_names = c(
    "consistency",
    "rec_sum",
    "sum_lower",
    "sum_upper",
    "rec_x_upper",
    "rec_x_lower"
  ),
  # Not returned by `grim_scalar()`, which would change what `grim()` returns:
  .cols_derived = list(exp_incon = grim_exp_incon)
)

The output has the key columns first, then any helper columns that were given, any columns of .args_by_row arguments, and consistency. Other columns of data follow it. Functions built on the mapper, such as function_map_seq(), read the columns left of consistency as the input to the test. The arguments of a call that apply to all rows, such as rounding, are recorded on the output; see scrutiny_meta().

Context and export

function_map() takes the place of function(): it is a function factory, or more precisely a function operator (Wickham 2019), like Vectorize().

To export a function made this way from your own package, follow this purrr FAQ, with scrutiny in the role of purrr:

schlim_map <- function(...) "dummy"

.onLoad <- function(lib, pkg) {
  schlim_map <<- scrutiny::function_map(
    .fn = schlim_scalar,
    .reported = c("y", "n"),
    .name_test = "SCHLIM"
  )
}

Identifying columns

Factory-made functions have one argument for each .reported value. If the columns of data have other names, specify these names via the arguments:

df2 <- df1
names(df2) <- c("foo", "bar")

schlim_map(df2, y = foo, n = bar)
#> # A tibble: 10 × 3
#>        y     n consistency
#>    <int> <int> <lgl>      
#>  1    16     3 TRUE       
#>  2    17     4 TRUE       
#>  3    18     5 TRUE       
#>  4    19     6 TRUE       
#>  5    20     7 FALSE      
#>  6    21     8 FALSE      
#>  7    22     9 FALSE      
#>  8    23    10 FALSE      
#>  9    24    11 FALSE      
#> 10    25    12 FALSE

A key column that is neither present in data nor identified via an argument is an error:

schlim_map(df2, y = foo)
#> Error in `schlim_map()`:
#> ! Column `n` is missing from `data`.
#> ✖ It should be a column of the input data frame.
#> ℹ Alternatively, specify the `n` argument of `schlim_map()` as the name of the
#>   equivalent column.

# With a wrong identification:
schlim_map(df2, n = mike)
#> Error in `schlim_map()`:
#> ! `mike` is not a column name of `data`.
#> ✖ The `n` argument of `schlim_map()` was specified as `mike`, but there is no
#>   column in `data` called `mike`.

A variable number of key columns

Some tests don’t have a fixed set of key columns. Think of a test that checks whether the values in any number of columns add up to the value in another column: how many columns go into each check depends on the data, not on the test.

Write the *_scalar() function so that it takes those values as a single vector argument, and name that argument in .reported_variadic:

sum_check_scalar <- function(parts, total, tolerance = 0) {
  abs(sum(parts) - total) <= tolerance
}

sum_check_map <- function_map(
  .fn = sum_check_scalar,
  .reported = "total",
  .reported_variadic = "parts",
  .name_test = "SUMCHECK"
)

The mapper then has a parts argument that selects columns using tidyselect syntax, alongside the ordinary total key argument:

df3 <- tibble::tibble(
  item_1 = c(10, 20, 30),
  item_2 = c(5, 5, 5),
  item_3 = c(1, 2, 3),
  total  = c(16, 27, 40)
)

sum_check_map(df3, parts = c(item_1, item_2, item_3))
#> # A tibble: 3 × 5
#>   item_1 item_2 item_3 total consistency
#>    <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl> <lgl>      
#> 1     10      5      1    16 TRUE       
#> 2     20      5      2    27 TRUE       
#> 3     30      5      3    40 FALSE

sum_check_map(df3, parts = starts_with("item"), tolerance = 3)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 5
#>   item_1 item_2 item_3 total consistency
#>    <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl> <lgl>      
#> 1     10      5      1    16 TRUE       
#> 2     20      5      2    27 TRUE       
#> 3     30      5      3    40 TRUE

Some points about this mode:

  • The selected columns are returned as themselves, so the output is as rectangular as any other mapper’s.

  • The variadic argument has no default. Selecting all remaining columns by default would quietly draw in columns such as identifiers.

  • The selection must not be empty or include a key or helper column. So parts = everything() is an error; write parts = !total instead.

  • .reported may be NULL if every key column is variadic.

  • Such a mapper cannot be wrapped by function_map_seq() or function_map_total_n(), which derive their arguments from .reported.

add_up_to_map() is made this way; see vignette("percentages-and-sums").

4. audit() and explain_map() methods

Basics

audit() is an S3 generic that summarizes the output of scrutiny’s mappers. Every mapper should have an audit() method, which returns descriptive statistics and nothing else. It dispatches on the class of the mapper’s output:

df1_tested <- schlim_map(df1)
class(df1_tested)
#> [1] "scrutiny_schlim_map" "tbl_df"              "tbl"                
#> [4] "data.frame"

Like the generic, the method takes data and .... It returns a tibble with at least these columns:

  1. all_cases, the total number of rows.

  2. incon_cases, the number of rows in which consistency is FALSE.

  3. emp_incon, the ratio of incon_cases to all_cases.

Add any other descriptive statistics that suit the test, such as means of output columns. All existing methods return a single row. Summaries by group come from audit()’s .by argument, which applies the method to each group, so the method itself needs no grouping.

Practical steps

The method is a function named audit plus a dot and your class. Call audit_cols_minimal() to create a tibble with the three required columns, and add further columns with dplyr::mutate() or similar:

audit.scrutiny_schlim_map <- function(data, ...) {
  audit_cols_minimal(data)
}

# This calls our new method:
audit(df1_tested)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 3
#>   all_cases incon_cases emp_incon
#>       <int>       <int>     <dbl>
#> 1        10           6       0.6

# This doesn't work because no method was defined:
audit(iris)
#> Error in `audit()`:
#> ! `audit()` has no method for `data`.
#> ✖ It has class <data.frame>.
#> ℹ See `?audit` for the functions whose output it summarizes.

Documentation

Document each audit() method on the page of its mapper, in a section called Summaries with audit() that lists the columns of its output. See ?grim_map for an example.

Explanations

explain_map() is a generic, too. Its method adds an explanation column, one string per row, which explain_print() prints:

explain_map.scrutiny_schlim_map <- function(data, ...) {
  verdict <- ifelse(data$consistency, "greater", "not greater")
  data$explanation <- paste0(
    data$y, " / 3 = ", round(data$y / 3, 2), ", which is ", verdict,
    " than ", data$n, "."
  )
  data
}

df1_tested |>
  dplyr::slice(4:5) |>
  explain_map() |>
  dplyr::pull(explanation)
#> [1] "19 / 3 = 6.33, which is greater than 6."    
#> [2] "20 / 3 = 6.67, which is not greater than 7."

A real explanation should give every number needed to check the result by hand, as grim_explain() does. Sequence and total-n output keeps the class of the basic mapper, so the method covers it as well.

5. Visualization function

How best to plot test results depends on the test: compare grim_plot_grid() and debit_plot(). (Granularity is crucial for GRIM but not for DEBIT.) Still, some conventions apply:

  1. Plots are based on ggplot2, following its advice on using ggplot2 in packages.
  2. The name is that of the test in lowercase, followed by _plot, and optionally a description, as in grim_plot_grid(). This doesn’t apply to methods for generics like ggplot2::autoplot().
  3. A function that plots mapper output takes it as its first argument, data, and checks that data has the mapper’s class, such as "scrutiny_debit_map".
  4. Map the key result column, such as consistency, to colour and fill, and add one ggplot2::scale_colour_manual() for both with aesthetics = c("colour", "fill"). Its values are "#0047ff" (blue) for consistent value sets and "#ff2a00" (red) for inconsistent ones, as in scrutiny’s own plots. Users change the colors by adding a scale of their own, not through arguments. (Plots of a single value set, such as grim_plot_line(), have no column to map, so they take the colors as color_* arguments.)
  5. Optional layers are controlled by logical arguments that start with show_, such as show_data in grim_plot_grid() or show_labels in debit_plot(). Only arguments of this kind start with show_, and they have defaults.

6. Sequence mapper

Introduction

A consistency test shows that reported values cannot all be correct, but not why. One common reason is a small error in computing or reporting: when Brown and Heathers (2017) reanalyzed data sets behind GRIM inconsistencies, they often found “a straightforward explanation, such as a minor error in the reported sample sizes, or a failure to report the exclusion of a participant” (p. 368).

Sequence mappers test for such errors. grim_map_seq(), grimmer_map_seq(), and debit_map_seq() vary each reported value by a few steps up and down and test the resulting value sets, so that consistent values near the reported ones are found without testing each candidate by hand.

Practical steps

Create sequence mappers from basic mappers with function_map_seq(). This is grimmer_map_seq():

grimmer_map_seq <- function_map_seq(
  .fn = grimmer_map,
  .reported = c("x", "sd", "n"),
  .name_test = "GRIMMER",
  # A standard deviation cannot be negative, but it can be `0`. The mean is
  # unbounded, as it is for GRIM. A sample SD needs two values, a population SD
  # only one:
  .var_bounds = list(
    n = function(args) c(sd_min_n(args$sd_meaning), NA),
    sd = c(0, NA)
  )
)

.var_bounds sets the least and greatest values to which each variable may be dispersed, with NA for an unbounded side. n always has a minimum of 1. A bound may also be a function of the mapper’s arguments, as with n here. .var, .dispersion, .out_min, .out_max, .include_reported, and .include_consistent set the defaults of the corresponding arguments of the new function; see ?function_map_seq.

A sequence mapper can be created in the same way from any other basic mapper. For SCHLIM:

schlim_map_seq <- function_map_seq(
  .fn = schlim_map,
  .reported = c("y", "n"),
  .name_test = "SCHLIM"
)

# Test dispersed sequences:
out_seq <- schlim_map_seq(df1)
out_seq
#> # A tibble: 120 × 6
#>        y     n consistency diff_var  case var  
#>    <int> <int> <lgl>          <int> <int> <chr>
#>  1    15     7 FALSE             -5     5 y    
#>  2    16     7 FALSE             -4     5 y    
#>  3    17     7 FALSE             -3     5 y    
#>  4    18     7 FALSE             -2     5 y    
#>  5    19     7 FALSE             -1     5 y    
#>  6    21     7 FALSE              1     5 y    
#>  7    22     7 TRUE               2     5 y    
#>  8    23     7 TRUE               3     5 y    
#>  9    24     7 TRUE               4     5 y    
#> 10    25     7 TRUE               5     5 y    
#> # ℹ 110 more rows

# Summarize:
audit(out_seq)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 12
#>       y     n consistency hits_total hits_y hits_n diff_y diff_y_up diff_y_down
#>   <int> <int> <lgl>            <int>  <int>  <int>  <int>     <int>       <int>
#> 1    20     7 FALSE                9      4      5      2         2          NA
#> 2    21     8 FALSE                6      2      4      4         4          NA
#> 3    22     9 FALSE                4      0      4     NA        NA          NA
#> 4    23    10 FALSE                3      0      3     NA        NA          NA
#> 5    24    11 FALSE                2      0      2     NA        NA          NA
#> 6    25    12 FALSE                2      0      2     NA        NA          NA
#> # ℹ 3 more variables: diff_n <int>, diff_n_up <int>, diff_n_down <int>

By default, a *_map_seq() function only creates sequences around inconsistent value sets, since its purpose is to shed light on inconsistencies. Override this with include_consistent = TRUE:

df1 |>
  schlim_map_seq(include_consistent = TRUE) |>
  audit()
#> # A tibble: 10 × 12
#>        y     n consistency hits_total hits_y hits_n diff_y diff_y_up diff_y_down
#>    <int> <int> <lgl>            <int>  <int>  <int>  <int>     <int>       <int>
#>  1    16     3 TRUE                14     10      4      1         1          -1
#>  2    17     4 TRUE                13      9      4      1         1          -1
#>  3    18     5 TRUE                11      7      4      1         1          -1
#>  4    19     6 TRUE                10      5      5      1         1          NA
#>  5    20     7 FALSE                9      4      5      2         2          NA
#>  6    21     8 FALSE                6      2      4      4         4          NA
#>  7    22     9 FALSE                4      0      4     NA        NA          NA
#>  8    23    10 FALSE                3      0      3     NA        NA          NA
#>  9    24    11 FALSE                2      0      2     NA        NA          NA
#> 10    25    12 FALSE                2      0      2     NA        NA          NA
#> # ℹ 3 more variables: diff_n <int>, diff_n_up <int>, diff_n_down <int>

audit() summarizes this output without a method of its own; the summaries differ between tests only in the key columns. Document them on the page of your *_map_seq() function as ?grim_map_seq does, in a section called Summaries with audit(). To export a function made by function_map_seq(), see section 3.

Dispersing single values

Sequence mappers build on seq_disperse(), which creates a numeric sequence centered around from. It takes the step size from the decimal places of from, so that a sequence around 4.1 proceeds in steps of 0.1. A number loses trailing zeros, so for a value like 5.30, state the step size with by or give from as a string:

seq_disperse(from = 4.1, dispersion = 1:3)
#> [1] 3.8 3.9 4.0 4.1 4.2 4.3 4.4

# Default for `dispersion` is `1:5`:
seq_disperse(from = 4.1)
#>  [1] 3.6 3.7 3.8 3.9 4.0 4.1 4.2 4.3 4.4 4.5 4.6

seq_disperse(from = 5.30, by = 0.01, dispersion = 1:3)
#> [1] 5.27 5.28 5.29 5.30 5.31 5.32 5.33
seq_disperse(from = "5.30", dispersion = 1:3)
#> [1] 5.27 5.28 5.29 5.30 5.31 5.32 5.33

seq_disperse_df() embeds the sequence as a tibble column.

7. Total-n mapper

Introduction

Group means and standard deviations are not always reported with their group sizes, but only with a total sample size. A test that requires the group sizes, such as GRIM, can then only be applied to hypothetical ways of splitting the total into two groups. This gives no definitive result, but it shows whether the reported values are consistent with at least some plausible group sizes (Bauer and Francis 2021).

Practical steps

function_map_total_n() creates functions that do this. See vignette("grim-in-depth"), section Unknown group sizes, for a case study. This is grimmer_map_total_n():

grimmer_map_total_n <- function_map_total_n(
  .fn = grimmer_map,
  .reported = c("x", "sd"), # not `n`
  .name_test = "GRIMMER",
  .n_min = function(args) sd_min_n(args$sd_meaning)
)

.n_min is the smallest group size. Like .var_bounds in function_map_seq(), it can be a function of the settings of the call: a group of 1 has no sample SD, but it does have a population SD.

.reported names the group statistics, each of which appears as two columns in the input, such as x1 and x2. .dispersion, .n_min, .n_max, and .constant are passed on to disperse_total(). It splits a total into pairs of hypothetical group sizes that add up to it, starting from half (or, for an odd total, from the two integers closest to half) and moving outward. It calls disperse() or disperse2() depending on parity; the two can also be called directly.

# With an even total...
disperse_total(n = 70)
#> # A tibble: 12 × 2
#>        n n_change
#>    <int>    <int>
#>  1    35        0
#>  2    35        0
#>  3    34       -1
#>  4    36        1
#>  5    33       -2
#>  6    37        2
#>  7    32       -3
#>  8    38        3
#>  9    31       -4
#> 10    39        4
#> 11    30       -5
#> 12    40        5

# ...and with an odd total:
disperse_total(n = 83)
#> # A tibble: 12 × 2
#>        n n_change
#>    <int>    <int>
#>  1    41        0
#>  2    42        0
#>  3    40       -1
#>  4    43        1
#>  5    39       -2
#>  6    44        2
#>  7    38       -3
#>  8    45        3
#>  9    37       -4
#> 10    46        4
#> 11    36       -5
#> 12    47        5

For SCHLIM:

schlim_map_total_n <- function_map_total_n(
  .fn = schlim_map,
  .reported = "y",
  .name_test = "SCHLIM"
)

# Example data:
df_groups_schlim <- tibble::tribble(
  ~y1 , ~y2 , ~n ,
   84 ,  37 , 29 ,
   61 ,  55 , 26
)

# Test dispersed sequences:
out_total_n <- schlim_map_total_n(df_groups_schlim)
out_total_n
#> # A tibble: 46 × 7
#>        y     n n_change consistency both_consistent  case dir  
#>    <dbl> <int>    <int> <lgl>       <lgl>           <int> <fct>
#>  1    84    14        0 TRUE        FALSE               1 forth
#>  2    37    15        0 FALSE       FALSE               1 forth
#>  3    84    13       -1 TRUE        FALSE               1 forth
#>  4    37    16        1 FALSE       FALSE               1 forth
#>  5    84    12       -2 TRUE        FALSE               1 forth
#>  6    37    17        2 FALSE       FALSE               1 forth
#>  7    84    11       -3 TRUE        FALSE               1 forth
#>  8    37    18        3 FALSE       FALSE               1 forth
#>  9    84    10       -4 TRUE        FALSE               1 forth
#> 10    37    19        4 FALSE       FALSE               1 forth
#> # ℹ 36 more rows

# Summarize:
audit(out_total_n)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 8
#>      y1    y2     n hits_total hits_forth hits_back scenarios_total hit_rate
#>   <dbl> <dbl> <int>      <int>      <int>     <int>           <int>    <dbl>
#> 1    84    37    29          4          0         4              12   0.3333
#> 2    61    55    26         11          6         5              11   1

As for sequence mappers, audit() needs no new method, but document its summaries on the page of your *_map_total_n() function, as ?grim_map_total_n does. To export such a function from a package, see section 3.

Wrap-up

This vignette generated four functions from a single-case test, three of them with scrutiny’s function factories, and added audit() and explain_map() methods by hand. The diagram below shows how the four derive from each other. Fields with bold margins are function factories; an arrow passing through one means that a new function is generated from an earlier one.

Here is an overview of scrutiny’s function factories:

Output function type Section here Function factory GRIM example function Predicate function
Basic mapper 3 function_map() grim_map() is_map_basic_df()
Sequence mapper 6 function_map_seq() grim_map_seq() is_map_seq_df()
Total-n mapper 7 function_map_total_n() grim_map_total_n() is_map_total_n_df()

The predicate functions return TRUE for the output of the respective factory-made functions. is_map_df() returns TRUE for all of them.
